title: Contemplatives in action
hook: early Jesuits described themselves as contemplatives in action

segments.voice: Yesterday, God in all things: the steam off a cup, a page of hard reading, a walk. Your line was all things. Where did the line catch you in a boring moment? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-three.

Here is a puzzle the first Jesuits had to solve. Catholic religious life had a beautiful rhythm: monks and nuns, and later friars, gathering in choir through the day to chant the psalms together. The bell rang, and everyone came in from the fields. Ignatius and his companions wanted something different. They wanted to be sent: to cities, to ports, to hospitals, to far countries, often alone. A bell in one chapel can't call a man who's on a ship. So how does a person pray when the job is to keep moving? Today's phrase is the answer they gave.
screen: `THE BELL CALLS THE CHOIR IN.` → `BUT WHAT IF YOU'RE ON A SHIP?` → `HOW DOES A TRAVELER PRAY?`

segments.voice: Contemplatives in action. The phrase is usually traced to Jerónimo Nadal, one of the early Jesuits, who traveled from house to house explaining the new order to its own members. Describing Ignatius, he said, in Latin, that he was contemplative even in action. Not first contemplative and then active, in two shifts. Both at once. So the new order made a choice that surprised people. The Jesuits did not gather in choir to chant the hours together the way monks and friars did. Each one still prayed, still went to Mass, still kept the daily examen. But the shape of the day was built for movement. That was not a judgment on the monasteries. The Church keeps both, and the Carmelites, coming up soon on this path, will show the other shape. It was a different shape for a different job. What holds it together is the idea from yesterday. If God is at work in all things, then the classroom, the sickroom and the road are not interruptions to prayer. They are where prayer goes. Saint Paul packs it into three words in the Douay-Rheims: "Pray without ceasing." Nobody can kneel without ceasing. But a person can carry a quiet awareness of God through a busy day, the way you carry a song in your head. Some readers worry this becomes an excuse: I'm too busy to pray, my work is my prayer. The early Jesuits answered that with the examen and the Exercises. Action stays prayer only if there's still a still point somewhere to return to. Motion and stillness, braided together.
screen: `NADAL: CONTEMPLATIVE EVEN IN ACTION.` · `NO CHOIR, BUILT FOR MOVEMENT.` · `THE ROAD IS WHERE PRAYER GOES.` · `STILL A STILL POINT TO RETURN TO.` · then, large: `PRAY WITHOUT CEASING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray while working, in a small way. Settle, and breathe. Choose one simple task you can do right where you are: folding a cloth, tidying a drawer, wiping a table, even straightening the things on your desk. Do it slowly, with full attention. With each movement, let a short phrase ride along. If you pray, it can be the name of Jesus, or Paul's pray without ceasing. If you don't, it can simply be: here, now. Notice the work and the awareness moving together. The bell holds the time.
Contemplatives in action. The early Jesuit ideal of praying in the middle of work and travel, not only apart from it, with the examen as the still point. Today's word.
Your line: prayer in motion. Today, pick one errand, a drive, a walk to the bus, a load of laundry, and let the line ride along with it. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Jesuits and people formed in Ignatian spirituality try to pray in the midst of work and travel, anchored by Mass, personal prayer and the daily examen.

fork.setup: you're one of the first Jesuits. other orders gather in choir through the day to chant the psalms. your work is to be sent anywhere. what do you do?
options: keep the choir and travel less.
drop choir, and pray on the move with Mass and the examen.
drop prayer and just work hard.
fork.reveal: the Jesuits did not keep choir. they built a day for movement, and kept a still point in Mass, personal prayer and the examen.

original.note: Latin: contemplative in action, Nadal's description of Ignatius.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fancy name for staying busy.
what it means: praying in the middle of work and travel, because God is at work in all things.
what a scholar hears: Nadal's description of Ignatius, and an order that did not chant the hours in choir.

notes: Attribution of 'contemplative in action' to Nadal is hedged as 'usually traced'; the Latin is commonly given as 'simul in actione contemplativus'. Confirm the wording and the Monumenta reference.
Nadal as one who traveled explaining the Constitutions to Jesuit houses: confirm.
Jesuits not keeping choir: Constitutions no. 586 and the Formula; confirm the citation number.
Original pronunciation uses ecclesiastical Latin; confirm.
The forward mention of the Carmelites anticipates days 1271 on; confirm it does not teach tomorrow's or a later day's content.
